questions.question: What is a Git branch and how is it implemented internally?
questions.title: What Is a Git Branch?
questions.direct_answer: A **Git branch** is a lightweight, movable **pointer** to a single commit. Creating one just writes a tiny file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a 40-character **commit hash** — it never copies your code, which is why branching is nearly instant. The **`HEAD`** pointer then tracks which branch you currently have checked out.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands a branch is a pointer to a commit, not a copy of files, and can connect that to HEAD and Git's shared object database
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing a branch duplicates the codebase, which makes freshers afraid to branch and unable to explain why branching is instant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that branch pointers are plain text files in .git/refs/heads/ and that all branches share one object database, so a hundred branches cost almost no disk

sections.title: A Branch Is a Pointer, Not a Copy
sections.content:
A **Git branch** is a lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit in your repository's history. It does **not** copy your files.

When you create a branch, Git writes a tiny (~40-byte) file under `.git/refs/heads/` containing a **commit hash** — a 40-character SHA-1 like `a3f2b9c...`. That's the entire branch. This is why branching is instant even on huge repos, and why you can have hundreds of branches for almost no disk cost: every branch shares the same underlying objects in `.git/objects/`.

As you commit, Git moves the current branch pointer forward to the newest commit. The special **`HEAD`** pointer tracks which branch you're on right now. So a branch is best understood as a label that slides along the commit graph as you work.

sections.title: How a Branch Works Internally
sections.content:
amber|Branch pointer|~A ref, not a copy|file in .git/refs/heads/|holds one commit hash|~40 bytes
blue|HEAD|~Your 'you are here'|points to current branch|moves when you switch|stored in .git/HEAD
emerald|Object database|~Shared by all branches|.git/objects/|commits, trees, blobs|no duplication
violet|Moving forward|~On each commit|branch pointer advances|HEAD follows|graph grows

sections.title: Create a Branch and Inspect the Pointer
sections.content:
```bash
# Create and switch to a feature branch (one command)
git switch -c feature-user-auth

# Make a change in a Spring Boot project and commit
git add src/main/java/com/example/UserService.java
git commit -m "feat: add user authentication service"

# The branch now points to the new commit
git log --oneline -1
# a3f2b9c (HEAD -> feature-user-auth) feat: add user authentication service

# Prove the branch is just a file holding a hash
cat .git/refs/heads/feature-user-auth
# a3f2b9c4d8e7f6a5b4c3d2e1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3
```

sections.title: Misconception: branching is 'heavy' so work stays on main
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher avoids branches, fearing they copy the repo
git switch main
# ...commits half-finished feature straight onto main...
git commit -m "WIP user auth, not done"
# main is now broken/unreleasable, and there's nothing to PR
```

sections.title: Reality: branches are cheap, so isolate every task
sections.content:
```bash
# Branching costs ~40 bytes — create one per task freely
git switch -c feature-user-auth
git commit -m "feat: add user authentication service"
# main stays clean and deployable; this branch becomes a PR
```
*Creating 100 branches barely touches disk because they all share `.git/objects/` — never hesitate to branch.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking branches copy files**: a branch is a 40-byte pointer; it shares the object database with every other branch.
- **Working directly on `main`**: bypasses review and CI and leaves half-done work on the production line — always branch.
- **Expecting all branches to move on commit**: only the *current* branch pointer (and `HEAD`) advances; the others stay put.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **A branch is a movable pointer** to a commit, stored as a tiny file in `.git/refs/heads/`.
- **Branching is instant** because nothing is copied.
- **`HEAD`** tracks the branch you currently have checked out.
- **All branches share** the `.git/objects/` database — many branches cost almost no disk.
- **On commit, only the current branch and `HEAD` move** forward.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A Git branch is a lightweight, movable pointer to a specific commit — it is not a copy of your codebase. The way I think about it is a bookmark: you're marking a position in the project's history, not duplicating the book. When you create a branch, Git just writes a small file under the dot-git refs heads folder, and inside that file is a forty-character commit hash. That's the whole branch, which is why creating one is basically instant even on a massive repository. As you make commits on that branch, Git moves the pointer forward to your latest commit, and the special HEAD pointer keeps track of which branch you're currently on. Because all branches share the same object database, you can have dozens or even hundreds of branches without using much disk space — they're just different labels pointing into the same set of objects. In practice this means you should branch freely, one branch per feature or bug fix, to keep main stable and let your team review your code through pull requests. The mistake freshers make is assuming branches are heavy operations that copy files, so they avoid them and end up committing straight to main. They're actually extremely cheap, so use them all the time.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'git checkout -b' and 'git switch -c' for creating branches?
questions.title: git checkout -b vs git switch -c
questions.direct_answer: Both create and move to a new branch, but **`git switch -c`** (Git 2.23+) is the modern, single-purpose command for branch operations, while **`git checkout -b`** is the older overloaded command that also restores files and detaches `HEAD`. Git split `checkout` into **`git switch`** (branches) and **`git restore`** (files) to remove that ambiguity, so `git switch -c` is clearer and safer for new work.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows modern Git split the overloaded checkout into switch and restore, and why that matters for clarity and safety
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing git switch and git restore exist, so the candidate uses checkout for everything from older tutorials
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that git restore took over file restoration, so each command now has one job, and that switch avoids checkout's accidental file-overwrite footgun

sections.title: Why Git Split checkout Into switch and restore
sections.content:
For years **`git checkout`** was Git's Swiss Army knife — it switched branches, created branches, restored files, and detached `HEAD`. The same verb doing wildly different things confused everyone, especially beginners.

In **Git 2.23 (2019)** the team introduced two focused commands: **`git switch`** for branch operations and **`git restore`** for file operations. Now `git switch -c <name>` creates and switches to a branch, and `git restore <file>` discards changes — each command has one clear job. `git checkout -b` still works for backward compatibility, but `git switch -c` is preferred because it's unambiguous and won't accidentally clobber a file if you mistype a branch name as a path.

sections.title: git checkout -b vs git switch -c
sections.content:
| Aspect | `git checkout -b` | `git switch -c` |
|---|---|---|
| **What it does** | create + switch to a branch | create + switch to a branch |
| **Introduced** | early Git (legacy) | Git 2.23 (2019) |
| **Scope** | overloaded — also restores files, detaches HEAD | single-purpose — branches only |
| **Safety** | a typo can overwrite a file | branch-focused, far less error-prone |
| **File restore** | `git checkout -- file` | use `git restore file` instead |
| **Use when** | legacy scripts/habits | all new work |

sections.title: Old checkout vs Modern split
sections.content:
rose|git checkout|~Overloaded Swiss-knife|switches branches|restores files|detaches HEAD
emerald|git switch|~Branches only|switch -c creates|switch moves|clear intent, safer
blue|git restore|~Files only|discard local edits|pull file from a commit|replaces checkout -- file
amber|Why it changed|~Single responsibility|added in Git 2.23|removes ambiguity|prevents accidental overwrite

sections.title: Overloaded checkout: same verb, dangerously different jobs
sections.content:
```bash
# Create a branch...
git checkout -b feature-payment

# ...but the SAME command also discards file changes:
git checkout -- OrderService.java   # silently wipes your edits!

# One verb for branches AND files = easy to trigger by accident
```

sections.title: Modern split: one verb per job
sections.content:
```bash
# Branch work -> git switch
git switch -c feature-payment   # create + switch
git switch main                 # move between branches

# File work -> git restore (clearly separate)
git restore OrderService.java   # discard local edits, on purpose
```
*Each command states its intent, so a branch typo can never quietly overwrite your files.*

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content: **Default to `git switch -c` for all new work** — `git switch -c feature-add-payment` is clear and safe, and pairing it with `git restore` for files keeps your mental model clean. **Use `git checkout` only for legacy compatibility** — older projects, scripts, or teammates' muscle memory. There's no functional downside to checkout, but switch/restore make your intent obvious and remove a class of accidental-overwrite bugs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not knowing `git switch` exists**: learning from pre-2019 tutorials leaves you fighting checkout's overloaded behavior.
- **Using checkout to discard files**: `git checkout -- file.java` works but `git restore file.java` says exactly what it does.
- **Mixing the two inconsistently**: switch for branches but checkout for files adds cognitive load — commit to switch + restore.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git switch -c`** — modern, single-purpose create-and-switch (Git 2.23+).
- **`git checkout -b`** — legacy, overloaded; also restores files and detaches HEAD.
- **`git restore`** — companion command that took over file restoration.
- **Single responsibility** makes the modern pair safer and clearer.
- **checkout still works** indefinitely for backward compatibility.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Both commands do the same thing — create a new branch and switch to it immediately. The difference is that git switch dash c is the modern, purpose-built command for branch operations, and git checkout dash b is the older overloaded one. The problem with checkout was that it did far too many jobs: it switched branches, created branches, restored files, and detached HEAD, all under the same verb. That confused a lot of people. So in Git 2.23, back in 2019, the team split it into two commands — git switch for branch operations and git restore for file operations. Now there's a clean separation: if you're working with branches you use switch, and if you're discarding or restoring files you use restore. The old checkout command still works for backward compatibility, so you'll see it everywhere in older tutorials and scripts. But for new work I'd reach for git switch dash c because the intent is obvious and it's safer — you can't accidentally overwrite a file when you only meant to create a branch, which was a real footgun with checkout. As a fresher, learning the modern pair, switch and restore, makes Git a lot less confusing as you go deeper.

questions.question: What is a feature branch workflow and why is it used?
questions.title: Feature Branch Workflow
questions.direct_answer: In the **feature branch workflow**, every feature or bug fix is built on its own short-lived branch off `main`, then merged back through a **pull request** after review. It keeps `main` always deployable, enables **parallel development** without conflicts, and makes **code review** a mandatory gate. It's the default workflow on virtually every professional team.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the day-to-day team workflow: branch off main, PR, review, merge — and why each step exists
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing directly to main in a team setting, or branching from a stale main and hitting avoidable conflicts later
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that short-lived feature branches plus pull requests give you parallel work AND a review checkpoint, and that you should pull main before branching

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One task = one short-lived branch** off `main`.
- **`main` is always deployable** — no half-finished work.
- **Pull requests** make review and CI a required gate before merge.
- **Parallel development** without devs blocking each other.
- **Pull `main` before branching**, and delete the branch after merge.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The feature branch workflow is the standard way teams collaborate with Git. The core rule is that you never commit directly to main. Every time you start a new feature or bug fix, you create a dedicated branch off main — so if I'm adding search to a Spring Boot app, I'd run git switch dash c feature add search. I do all my work on that branch, making commits as I go. When it's ready, I push the branch and open a pull request. That pull request is where teammates review my code and where CI runs the tests before anything reaches main. Once it's approved and green, I merge into main and delete the feature branch, because its job is done. This solves a few problems at once. It keeps main stable and always deployable, so you never break it with half-finished work. It enables parallel development — I can work on authentication while you work on payments, and we don't step on each other. And it makes code review a required step, which really improves quality. A couple of mistakes freshers make: committing straight to main, which skips all of this, and branching off a stale main without pulling first, which leads to nasty conflicts later. The fix is simple — always pull main before you branch, and keep each branch focused on one task.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Both create and move to a new branch, but **`git switch -c`** (Git 2.23+) is the modern, single-purpose command for branch operations, while **`git checkout -b`** is the older overloaded command that also restores files and detaches `HEAD`.

Git split `checkout` into **`git switch`** (branches) and **`git restore`** (files) to remove that ambiguity, so `git switch -c` is clearer and safer for new work.

In the **feature branch workflow**, every feature or bug fix is built on its own short-lived branch off `main`, then merged back through a **pull request** after review. It keeps `main` always deployable, enables **parallel development** without conflicts, and makes **code review** a mandatory gate. It's the default workflow on virtually every professional team.

Believing a branch duplicates the codebase, which makes freshers afraid to branch and unable to explain why branching is instant

sections.title: The Feature Branch Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[git switch main
git pull] --> B[git switch -c
feature-x] B --> C[code + commit] C --> D[git push
feature-x] D --> E[open PR
review + CI] E --> F[merge to main] F --> G[delete branch] ```

sections.title: The Workflow Step by Step
sections.content:
```bash
# 1. Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull origin main

# 2. Create a feature branch
git switch -c feature-add-customer-search

# 3. Develop + commit (e.g. a new CustomerSearchService)
git add src/main/java/com/example/service/CustomerSearchService.java
git commit -m "feat: add case-insensitive customer search"

# 4. Push the branch to the remote
git push origin feature-add-customer-search

# 5. Open a pull request -> review + CI run
# 6. After approval, merge to main, then clean up
git switch main && git pull origin main
git branch -d feature-add-customer-search
```

sections.title: Anti-pattern: committing straight to main
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher treats main as a personal scratch pad
git switch main
git add .
git commit -m "add search + random unrelated tweak"
git push origin main
# No review, breaks CI expecting PRs, conflicts with teammates pushing to main
```

sections.title: Correct: one task, one short-lived branch, one PR
sections.content:
```bash
git switch main && git pull origin main   # always start fresh
git switch -c feature-add-customer-search
git commit -am "feat: add case-insensitive customer search"
git push origin feature-add-customer-search
# Open a PR -> teammates review, CI runs, then merge
```
*One focused branch per task, pulled from a fresh main, keeps conflicts small and reviews meaningful.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Committing directly to `main`**: skips review, breaks CI, and causes conflicts — always branch.
- **One giant long-lived branch**: a single `my-work` branch with unrelated changes defeats isolation; one task per branch.
- **Branching from a stale `main`**: not running `git pull` first guarantees painful conflicts later.
- **Self-merging without review**: approving your own PR throws away the safety net the workflow exists for.

questions.question: How do you list, create, and delete branches in Git?
questions.title: Managing Git Branches: List, Create, Delete
questions.direct_answer: Use **`git branch`** to list local branches, **`git branch -a`** to include remote-tracking branches, **`git switch -c <name>`** (or `git branch <name>`) to create, and **`git branch -d <name>`** to delete a merged branch. The lowercase **`-d`** is safe — it refuses to drop unmerged work — while **`-D`** force-deletes regardless.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the everyday branch commands and the safety difference between -d and -D
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for -D as a 'stronger delete' and discarding unmerged commits, or forgetting -a when hunting for a teammate's remote branch
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that -d protects you by refusing to delete unmerged branches, that force-deleted commits are often recoverable via reflog, and that -r lists remote-tracking branches only

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`git branch`** lists local; **`-a`** adds remote-tracking; **`-r`** is remote-only.
- **`git switch -c <name>`** creates and switches in one step.
- **`git branch -d`** is safe — refuses unmerged branches.
- **`git branch -D`** force-deletes regardless — use cautiously.
- **`git reflog`** can often recover commits after an accidental force-delete.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: There are three everyday operations: listing, creating, and deleting branches. To list them, you run git branch, which shows your local branches with an asterisk next to the one you're on. If you also want to see remote branches — say, something a teammate pushed — you add dash a, so git branch dash a, and that shows local plus remote-tracking branches. To create a branch, you can use git branch with a name to just create it, but more commonly you'd use git switch dash c with a name, which creates the branch and switches to it in one step. For deleting, there's an important safety distinction. Lowercase git branch dash d deletes a branch, but it's safe — it refuses if the branch has commits that haven't been merged yet, which protects you from losing work. Uppercase dash D force-deletes regardless, so you should only use it when you're certain you don't need that work. Always try the lowercase version first. In practice you'd delete feature branches after they're merged to keep your branch list tidy. The mistakes freshers make are reaching for dash D as if it's just a stronger delete and losing commits, and forgetting dash a when looking for a remote branch, so they think it doesn't exist when it's actually on origin. And if you ever do force-delete something by accident, git reflog can usually help you recover the commit.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Both create and move to a new branch, but **`git switch -c`** (Git 2.23+) is the modern, single-purpose command for branch operations, while **`git checkout -b`** is the older overloaded command that also restores files and detaches `HEAD`.

Git split `checkout` into **`git switch`** (branches) and **`git restore`** (files) to remove that ambiguity, so `git switch -c` is clearer and safer for new work.

Use **`git branch`** to list local branches, **`git branch -a`** to include remote-tracking branches, **`git switch -c <name>`** (or `git branch <name>`) to create, and **`git branch -d <name>`** to delete a merged branch. The lowercase **`-d`** is safe — it refuses to drop unmerged work — while **`-D`** force-deletes regardless.

Believing a branch duplicates the codebase, which makes freshers afraid to branch and unable to explain why branching is instant

sections.title: Branch Commands at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|List|~See what exists|git branch (local)|git branch -a (all)|git branch -r (remote)
emerald|Create|~Start new work|git branch name|git switch -c name|switch -c also moves you
rose|Delete|~Clean up|git branch -d (safe)|git branch -D (force)|-d refuses unmerged work
amber|Inspect|~Know your context|* marks current branch|run before committing|avoids wrong-branch commits

sections.title: List, Create, and Delete in One Session
sections.content:
```bash
# List local branches (current marked with *)
git branch
#   feature-payment
# * main

# Include remote-tracking branches
git branch -a
# * main
#   remotes/origin/main
#   remotes/origin/feature-payment

# Create + switch in one command
git switch -c feature-add-notifications

# After the PR merges, delete safely from main
git switch main
git branch -d feature-payment        # works only if merged

# Safe delete refuses unmerged work:
git branch -d bugfix-wip
# error: branch 'bugfix-wip' is not fully merged

# Force delete only if you're sure
git branch -D bugfix-wip             # use with caution
```

sections.title: Mistake: force-deleting and losing unmerged commits
sections.content:
```bash
# Fresher treats -D as 'delete harder' and skips the safety check
git branch -D feature-half-done
# Unmerged commits are gone from branch refs
# (recoverable via reflog only if you act fast)
```

sections.title: Safe: let -d guard your work
sections.content:
```bash
# Try the safe delete first
git branch -d feature-half-done
# error: not fully merged  <- Git just saved you

# Merge or back it up first, THEN delete
git switch main && git merge feature-half-done
git branch -d feature-half-done      # now safe
```
*If you ever do force-delete by accident, `git reflog` can usually recover the lost commit hash.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `-D` blindly**: it skips the unmerged-work safety check and can lose commits — try `-d` first.
- **Not cleaning up merged branches**: stale branches pile up and clutter `git branch` — delete after merge.
- **Forgetting `-a`**: plain `git branch` hides remote branches, so a teammate's pushed branch looks 'missing'.

questions.question: What is the HEAD pointer in Git?
questions.title: The HEAD Pointer in Git
questions.direct_answer: **`HEAD`** is a special pointer that marks your current position — the branch (or commit) you have checked out. It usually points to a branch via `.git/HEAD` (e.g. `ref: refs/heads/main`) and moves automatically when you switch branches or commit. Checking out a raw commit hash puts you in **detached HEAD** state, where new commits belong to no branch.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands HEAD as a local 'current position' pointer and can explain detached HEAD state
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing HEAD with the remote or with main specifically, or panicking in detached HEAD without knowing commits there can be lost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that HEAD is stored in .git/HEAD as a ref, that HEAD~1 references prior commits, and that you save detached-HEAD work by branching from it

sections.title: HEAD Is Your 'You Are Here' Marker
sections.content:
**`HEAD`** is the pointer Git uses to track your current position — which branch or commit you currently have checked out. Most of the time it points to a **branch name**, and that branch points to a commit.

It's stored as a file at `.git/HEAD`, usually containing something like `ref: refs/heads/main`. When you commit, Git moves both `HEAD` and the current branch forward together. When you `git switch` to another branch, `HEAD` updates to point at it. Commands like `git log` start from `HEAD`. Understanding it matters because Git error messages constantly mention `HEAD`, and concepts like **detached HEAD** only make sense once you see that `HEAD` is just a pointer that can aim at different things.

sections.title: HEAD States at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Normal HEAD|~Points to a branch|.git/HEAD = ref: refs/heads/main|moves with commits|the everyday case
amber|Detached HEAD|~Points to a commit|happens on checkout <hash>|new commits orphaned|fine for read-only
emerald|Relative refs|~Walk backwards|HEAD~1 = one commit back|HEAD~3 = three back|used in reset/diff
rose|Local only|~Per-developer|not synced to origin|each repo has its own|nothing remote about it

sections.title: Normal vs Detached HEAD
sections.content:
```bash
# Normal: HEAD points to a branch
git switch main
cat .git/HEAD            # ref: refs/heads/main

git commit -am "feat: add order persistence"
git log --oneline -1
# a3f2b9c (HEAD -> main) feat: add order persistence

# Detached HEAD: check out a raw commit hash
git checkout a3f2b9c
# Note: switching to 'a3f2b9c'. You are in 'detached HEAD' state.
git log --oneline -1
# a3f2b9c (HEAD) feat: add order persistence   <- no branch name!

# Save detached work by branching, or just go back
git switch -c experiment   # keep any commits made here
git switch main            # back to normal
```

sections.title: Trap: committing in detached HEAD and losing it
sections.content:
```bash
git checkout a3f2b9c          # detached HEAD
git commit -am "fix: quick experiment"
git switch main              # walked away...
# The experiment commit belongs to no branch -> easy to lose
```

sections.title: Fix: branch first, then commit
sections.content:
```bash
git checkout a3f2b9c          # detached HEAD
git switch -c experiment      # attach a branch BEFORE committing
git commit -am "fix: quick experiment"
# Now the commit lives on 'experiment' and is safe
```
*Detached HEAD is safe for read-only investigation — just create a branch before making commits you care about.*

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing `HEAD` with `main`**: `HEAD` is wherever you currently are; on `feature-auth` it points there, not to `main`.
- **Thinking `HEAD` is remote**: it's purely local — each clone has its own `HEAD`.
- **Panicking in detached HEAD**: it's safe to look around; just branch before committing anything you want to keep.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`HEAD` marks your current branch/commit** — your 'you are here'.
- **Normally points to a branch** via `.git/HEAD` (`ref: refs/heads/...`).
- **Moves automatically** on commit and on `git switch`.
- **Detached HEAD** = pointing at a raw commit; new commits there are orphaned unless you branch.
- **`HEAD~1`, `HEAD~2`** reference earlier commits; `HEAD` is local-only.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: HEAD is a special pointer in Git that tracks your current position in the repository — it's basically your 'you are here' marker. At any moment, HEAD points to whatever branch you currently have checked out, and that branch points to a commit. Git stores HEAD as a file in the dot-git folder, and inside it you'll usually see something like 'ref colon refs slash heads slash main', meaning HEAD is pointing to the main branch. When you make a commit, Git automatically moves both HEAD and your current branch forward to the new commit. When you switch branches, HEAD moves to point at the new branch. This is how Git always knows where you are and where new commits should go. HEAD shows up constantly in Git messages, like 'HEAD is now at' some commit, and once you know it's just your position marker, those messages make sense. One special case is detached HEAD state. That happens when you check out a specific commit hash instead of a branch name, so HEAD points directly at that commit rather than a branch. It's called detached because you're not on any branch. That's totally fine for looking at old code, but if you make commits there, they don't belong to any branch and can be lost. So if you want to keep work done in detached HEAD, you create a branch from that point first. A common mistake freshers make is thinking HEAD is the same as main or that it has something to do with the remote — it doesn't. HEAD is purely local and just tracks wherever you currently are.

items: Normally HEAD points to a branch and moves forward when you commit.
If you check out a raw commit hash, you're in detached HEAD state.
HEAD is local only — it has nothing to do with the remote.

beats.text: If I check out an old commit to investigate a bug, HEAD detaches and points straight at that commit. If I want to keep any changes I make there, I create a branch first, otherwise those commits can get lost.

items: Don't confuse HEAD with main or with the remote.
Don't commit in detached HEAD without branching first.
